strings.hist.soviet.secret_protocol.title: The secret additional protocol to the Hitler–Stalin Pact
strings.hist.soviet.secret_protocol.text: In the night of 23 to 24 August 1939 the foreign ministers Ribbentrop and Molotov signed in Moscow a non-aggression treaty dated 23 August, together with a secret additional protocol. It partitioned Poland and assigned Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere of interest and, initially, Lithuania to the German one. It only became public after the war: German microfilm copies had survived; newspapers printed the text in 1946, the US State Department in 1948. For decades the USSR called the documents forgeries. Only on 24 December 1989 did the Congress of People’s Deputies of the USSR acknowledge the protocol’s existence, condemn it and declare it invalid from the outset. In October 1992 Russia presented the Soviet originals publicly for the first time.
strings.hist.soviet.katyn.title: Katyn 1940: what the files prove
strings.hist.soviet.katyn.text: On the proposal of NKVD chief Lavrentiy Beria, the Politburo decided on 5 March 1940 to have Polish prisoners of war and detainees shot. From April 1940 the NKVD killed officers, policemen, officials and other prisoners in the Katyn forest near Smolensk, in Kalinin (now Tver), in Kharkiv and elsewhere; a KGB note of 1959 gives 21,857 shot. After German authorities had publicised the mass graves at Katyn in 1943, a Soviet commission under Nikolai Burdenko declared in January 1944 that Germans had killed the prisoners in 1941. Only on 13 April 1990 did the Soviet Union, through the TASS agency, admit the responsibility of Beria and the NKVD. On 14 October 1992 Russia handed Poland documents from the secret file “Package No. 1”, among them the Politburo decision.
strings.hist.soviet.deportations.title: The deportation of entire peoples, 1941–1944
strings.hist.soviet.deportations.text: From August 1941 the NKVD deported almost 900,000 Soviet Germans to Siberia and Kazakhstan. In 1943/44 it carried off in freight trains entire peoples whom Moscow accused wholesale of treason, among them the Karachays, Kalmyks, Chechens and Ingush (almost half a million in February 1944), the Balkars and the Crimean Tatars. By 1948 the authorities in the special settlements had recorded the deaths of around a quarter of the deportees from the North Caucasus, just under a fifth of those deported from Crimea and 17 to 18 per cent of the Kalmyks. On 14 November 1989 the Supreme Soviet of the USSR declared the deportations unlawful and criminal. A law of the RSFSR of 26 April 1991 rehabilitated the “repressed peoples” and states that they were subjected to genocide and slander.
strings.hist.soviet.novocherkassk.title: Novocherkassk 1962: shots fired at strikers
strings.hist.soviet.novocherkassk.text: On 1 June 1962 workers at the electric locomotive works in Novocherkassk went on strike against higher prices for meat and butter and raised work quotas. On 2 June thousands marched to the seat of the city’s party leadership; soldiers fired into the crowd. According to the KGB, 26 people died and 87 were wounded; other sources give 24 dead. The dead were buried in remote cemeteries without their families’ knowledge. Seven participants were sentenced to death and executed, more than 100 others to prison terms. Only in the late Gorbachev era did Soviet media report on it. From 1990 the public prosecutor’s office examined the case; in May 1992 the Supreme Soviet of Russia condemned the crushing of a peaceful demonstration. In 1994 the exhumed dead were laid to rest in Novocherkassk.
strings.hist.soviet.kyshtym.title: Kyshtym 1957: the nuclear accident kept secret
strings.hist.soviet.kyshtym.text: On 29 September 1957, at the Mayak plutonium plant near the secret city of Chelyabinsk-40, the cooling of a tank of highly radioactive waste failed; the tank exploded. Around 740 petabecquerels were released; 74 PBq came down outside the site on a strip some 300 kilometres long, the East Urals Trace. Around 10,000 people from more than 20 villages were resettled. The Soviet authorities kept the accident secret. In 1976 the biologist Zhores Medvedev, living in exile in London, made it known in the West in the journal New Scientist. Only in June 1989 did the TASS agency officially confirm the explosion. Chelyabinsk-40 was one of the closed nuclear cities of the USSR; today the city is called Ozyorsk.
strings.hist.soviet.gulag.title: The Gulag in figures: what the archives show
strings.hist.soviet.gulag.text: Since 1989, figures from the files of the GULAG camp administration have been published: first the historian Viktor Zemskov presented statistics, then in 1993 an archive-based study followed, written with J. Arch Getty and Gábor Rittersporn. In the Stalin era some 18 million people passed through the camps and prisons of the Gulag; probably another 6 to 7 million were sent into exile. At Stalin’s death in 1953 about 2.5 million were held in camps and colonies. At least 1.6 million deaths in the camps are documented. The files are considered incomplete, partly because camps released the dying. Other estimates give around 2.7 million dead. Golfo Alexopoulos (2017) describes the camps as often run like death camps; she includes those who died shortly after release and arrives at far higher, disputed figures.
strings.hist.soviet.great_terror.title: The Great Terror 1937/38: Order No. 00447
strings.hist.soviet.great_terror.text: On 30 July 1937 NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov signed the secret Order No. 00447. It set quotas for each region, initially some 270,000 people, around 76,000 of them to be shot; troikas passed sentence without the accused present. By November 1938 some 767,000 people had been sentenced under this order and 387,000 shot – by other calculations up to 820,000 and 445,000. Official figures for 1937/38: over 1.5 million arrests and 681,692 death sentences; historians from Memorial give at least 1.7 million arrested and over 700,000 shot. After Khrushchev’s fall in 1964, rehabilitation largely came to a halt; only on 16 January 1989 did a decree overturn, with exceptions, the sentences of the extrajudicial bodies. The order was not published until June 1992.
strings.hist.soviet.holodomor.title: Holodomor: the famine of 1932/33 in Ukraine
strings.hist.soviet.holodomor.text: In 1932/33 millions of people starved to death in Ukraine. Forced collectivisation and excessive grain quotas had preceded it; when quotas were not met, other foodstuffs were confiscated as well. On 22 January 1933 Moscow forbade the peasants of Ukraine and the Kuban to leave their famine-stricken areas. Estimates mostly lie at 3 to 4 million dead; a demographic study of 2015 arrives at 3.9 million. In Kazakhstan, too, over a million people died in 1930–33. The Soviet Union denied the famine for decades; only in 1987 was it officially mentioned in Ukraine, and in January 1990 the Communist Party of Ukraine released files for publication. Ukraine classified the Holodomor as genocide in 2006, the Bundestag and the European Parliament in 2022; researchers debate this classification.
